report.summary: Reviewed chunk 1 of mutate.py: docstring claims, filter constants, coverage reader, Mutant dataclass, equivalence check, tree-mutation operators.
risks: covered_lines | medium | claims to read coverage DB but uses SQLite line_bits layout without verifying schema; if schema differs, silently returns {} | add schema validation or document exact coverage DB format
covered_lines | medium | mode=ro URI may fail on non-URI SQLite builds; fallback to normal connect needed | test on target SQLite version
_code_fingerprint | low | includes co_names and co_varnames; renaming a local variable changes fingerprint, so equivalence may be under-detected | verify with variable-rename mutant
_fn_source | medium | returns empty string for lines; unused second element, likely dead code | confirm caller usage in chunk 2
_mutate_tree | medium | DROP_CALL with single-statement body is not handled in this chunk, may be incomplete | inspect chunk 2 for continuation
trivially_equivalent | low | compile() may succeed on code with different semantics due to name resolution; bytecode identity is conservative, as stated | acceptable per docstring
CHANGE_CONSTANT | low | includes string constants; docstring says display constants filtered elsewhere, but no filtering in this chunk | check chunk 2 for display constant filtering
WEAKEN_COMPARISON | low | only first operator; chained comparisons not fully handled | inspect chunk 2
covered_lines | low | returns {} for any DB error, conflating 'no coverage' with 'unreadable' | distinguish error from empty
trivially_equivalent | low | catches only SyntaxError/ValueError, not other compile errors | acceptable per docstring
todos: Inspect chunk 2 for DROP_CALL single-statement handling and remaining operators
Check _code_fingerprint exclusion of line/filename only; confirm co_positions not needed

claims.text: deterministic — a seed picks the sites, so a claim is reproducible.
claims.why: _mutate_tree uses rng.choice(sites) where rng is a random.Random instance passed in; the caller supplies the seed elsewhere (not in this chunk). The mechanism is deterministic given a seed.

claims.text: Every mutant is checked to still PARSE. A mutant that breaks syntax is not a defect, it is a typo, and any tool would catch it — counting those would inflate the score for free.
claims.why: _mutate_tree parses fn_src with ast.parse and returns None on SyntaxError; it also returns None if no sites are found. The generated source is produced by ast.unparse, which yields valid Python.

claims.text: Each rejection is COUNTED and named, so the filter can be audited instead of trusted.
claims.why: Line ~48 comment claims each rejection is counted and named, but this chunk shows no counting mechanism: no counter, no log, no return of rejection reasons. The filters are only constants and helper predicates; no audit trail exists in this chunk.

claims.text: A mutant here can never be a product defect.
claims.why: The constants SKIP_PATH_PARTS, SKIP_FUNCTIONS, _DISPLAY_CALLS, GUARD_NAMES are defined, but the actual filtering logic that uses them is not in this chunk. Whether they are applied correctly cannot be verified here.

claims.text: Cosmetic or self-describing methods: a changed repr is not a defect worth catching, and mutating one only teaches the detector to fire on noise.
claims.why: SKIP_FUNCTIONS is defined, but the filtering logic that uses it is not in this chunk.

claims.text: Constants whose value is display text, not behaviour. Changing a log message or a docstring is not a defect; it is a typo with no consequence.
claims.why: _DISPLAY_CALLS is defined and _is_display_constant uses it, but the integration into mutation selection is not in this chunk.

claims.text: Real incidents in the hand-written corpus were all removals of exactly this kind of code, so a site matching it is worth far more than a random one. This is a PRIOR on where defects live, not a correctness claim.
claims.why: GUARD_NAMES is defined and _looks_like_a_guard uses it, but the prior weighting in site selection is not in this chunk.

claims.text: A mutant on a line no test reaches is a GUARANTEED survivor: it cannot be caught by the gate, so measuring it only dilutes the score. This reads a coverage database if one is present and returns {} if not — and the caller must treat {} as "unknown", never as "nothing is covered".
claims.why: covered_lines returns {} if no DB file exists or on any sqlite/OS error, and the docstring explicitly instructs caller to treat {} as unknown. The function does read a coverage DB and returns a dict of covered lines.

claims.text: One generated defect. Field-compatible with the hand-written corpus's Mutation where it matters (id, defect_class, file), so the same measurement code reads both.
claims.why: The Mutant dataclass has fields id, defect_class, file, function, line, before, after, operator, and find/replace properties. Compatibility with an external Mutation class cannot be verified from this chunk alone.

claims.text: True if the two sources compile to IDENTICAL bytecode.
claims.why: The function compiles both sources and compares _code_fingerprint(a) == _code_fingerprint(b). The fingerprint includes co_code, constants, names, varnames, argcounts, and flags, which is a structural bytecode identity check.

claims.text: TRIVIAL COMPILER EQUIVALENCE, the cheap half of the equivalent-mutant problem. A mutant that compiles to the same code object cannot change behaviour, so it is undetectable by ANY method -- a perfect test suite, a perfect graph delta, a human. Counting such mutants in a denominator silently lowers every score for a reason that has nothing to do with the detector.
claims.why: The function compares bytecode fingerprints; identical fingerprints imply identical code objects (modulo line/filename), which cannot change behavior. The claim is accurate for the implemented mechanism.

claims.text: The literature puts the equivalent-mutant rate at roughly 10-40% (Jia & Harman's 2011 survey, per a research pass on 2026-07-30 -- the attribution is SECOND-HAND and unverified here; the filter below is not, because it is executed).
claims.why: The literature claim is external and explicitly marked as unverified; the chunk cannot verify it. The filter execution is verifiable and kept.

claims.text: Compilation is not execution: compile() builds a code object and runs nothing, so this is safe on arbitrary repository source.
claims.why: The function uses compile() only, which parses and compiles without executing. However, compile() can raise SyntaxError/ValueError, which are caught.

claims.text: Structural fingerprint of a code object, recursing into nested ones. Names and constants are included because a mutant that only changes a constant DOES change behaviour; what is excluded is line-number tables and filenames, which differ for reasons that are not the program.
claims.why: The function includes co_code, constants (recursed), co_names, co_varnames, co_argcount, co_kwonlyargcount, and co_flags with 0x20 stripped. It does not include co_filename or co_firstlineno. This matches the claim.

claims.text: (exact source of the function, its lines) or None if it cannot be sliced.
claims.why: Line ~205: The function returns "".join(lines[start:end]), "" which is a tuple (source, empty string). The docstring says 'its lines' but the second element is always empty string, not the lines. The implementation does not return the lines as claimed; it returns an empty string.

claims.text: Uses ast.unparse on the whole function, which normalises formatting. That is FINE for this purpose and worth stating: the measurement compares the mutant against its own unparsed original, never against the raw file, so normalisation cannot masquerade as a change.
claims.why: The function uses ast.unparse(tree) to produce the mutated source. The claim about normalisation being fine is a design statement; the code does use ast.unparse. The comparison against unparsed original is not in this chunk but is plausible.

claims.text: AFTER the docstring, never before. Inserting ahead of it demotes the docstring from body[0] to an ordinary string expression, which makes a LITERAL appear out of nowhere -- an artefact of the generator that was measured suppressing detection of this operator from ~100% to 37%.
claims.why: The code explicitly removes the leading docstring if present, then inserts ast.Return(value=None) after the head (which is the docstring). The insertion is after the docstring, as claimed.

claims.text: The filter below is not, because it is executed.
claims.why: The filter (the bytecode comparison) is executed in this function, unlike the literature attribution which is not.

claims.text: A mutant that breaks syntax is not a defect, it is a typo, and any tool would catch it — counting those would inflate the score for free.
claims.why: _mutate_tree returns None on SyntaxError, so such mutants are not generated. Any mutant produced by ast.unparse will parse, so the claim holds.

observations.what: The comment 'Each rejection is COUNTED and named' is not implemented in this chunk; no counting mechanism exists.
_fn_source returns an empty string as the second tuple element, contradicting the docstring's 'its lines'.
covered_lines may silently return {} on unreadable DB or schema mismatch, which could be misinterpreted as 'no coverage' despite the docstring's warning.
_code_fingerprint includes co_names and co_varnames, so renaming a local variable changes the fingerprint, potentially marking a semantically equivalent mutant as non-equivalent.
The DROP_CALL branch appears incomplete in this chunk: it only collects sites but the actual removal logic is cut off at the end.
observations.where: end of chunk in _mutate_tree DROP_CALL branch

observations.what: CHANGE_CONSTANT includes string constants without filtering display constants; _is_display_constant is defined but not used here.
WEAKEN_COMPARISON only inspects the first operator of a Compare node, so chained comparisons are not fully handled.
